common_name: Girard's Fuchsia Azalea (Hot Reddish-Pink Compact Girard Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Girard's Fuchsia is a dense, compact Girard hybrid grown for vivid fuchsia-purple color against glossy dark foliage.

directions: Girard's Fuchsia was hybridized by Peter Girard Sr. at Girard Nurseries in Geneva, Ohio, part of his line of cold-hardy, compact evergreen azaleas, and it covers itself each spring in brilliant fuchsia-purple single flowers against glossy dark green foliage. The dense, rounded habit works well in foundation plantings, woodland borders, low informal hedges, and large containers. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, mulch to keep roots cool, and prune only right after flowering since next year's buds set soon afterward.

common_name: Girard's Hot Shot Azalea (Fiery Orange-Scarlet Compact Girard Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; Hot Shot is a compact Girard hybrid with fiery reddish-orange, dark-spotted flowers and good fall foliage color.

directions: Girard's Hot Shot bears 3-inch, dark reddish-orange flowers marked with dark red spotting in dense mid-season clusters, set against glossy dark green foliage that turns rich red in fall. Part of Peter Girard's cold-hardy Ohio breeding line, it keeps a rounded, compact habit well suited to foundation beds and mixed shrub borders where larger Southern Indica types would overwhelm the space. Grow in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade and prune immediately after bloom, since next year's flower buds form shortly afterward.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Girard's Pleasant White Azalea (Large White Upright Girard Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; Pleasant White is a larger, upright Girard hybrid that benefits from more room than compact Girard selections.

directions: Introduced from a 1962 cross of Girard's own 'Kathy Ann' and 'Clara Marie', Pleasant White bears heavy midseason flushes of 2.5-3 inch white single flowers with gently wavy margins on an upright, more vigorous habit than most other Girard hybrids. Its larger ultimate size and bolt-upright branching suit it to shrub borders and taller foundation plantings rather than low edging. Grow in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and prune right after flowering since buds for the following spring set soon afterward.
sources: University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Plant of the Week

common_name: Girard's National Beauty Azalea (Deep Pink Low-Spreading Girard Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; National Beauty is a low, spreading Girard hybrid with large deep green leaves and profuse deep pink flowers.

directions: Girard's National Beauty produces an abundance of deep pink, wavy-edged, funnel-shaped flowers 2 to 2.5 inches across in midseason, held against large, glossy, deep green leaves that take on a reddish cast in fall and winter. Its low, spreading form and compact stature make it useful for mass plantings and informal low hedges where a wider, denser Girard selection is wanted. Site in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade and prune only immediately after bloom to avoid removing next year's buds.
sources: American Rhododendron Society Hybrid Azalea Database

common_name: Nancy of Robinhill Azalea (Light Pink Double Robin Hill Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Nancy of Robinhill is considered one of the finest Robin Hill introductions, with unusually large hose-in-hose double blooms.

directions: Named by Robert Gartrell for his wife, Nancy of Robinhill is widely considered one of the best Robin Hill azaleas, bearing large, 3.5-inch, light pink hose-in-hose double flowers with an occasional deeper blotch in mid to late May. Like other Robin Hill selections it combines a compact, low-mounding habit with unusually large flowers for a plant of its size, making it a strong choice for foundation plantings or underplanting taller shrubs. Grow in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and prune immediately after bloom since flower buds set on the current season's growth.
sources: Journal of the American Rhododendron Society

common_name: Gwenda Azalea (Pale Pink Wavy-Margined Robin Hill Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Gwenda is a later-blooming Robin Hill azalea with pale pink, wavy-margined single flowers.

directions: Gwenda opens pale pink, single flowers with distinctively wavy margins in early June, making it one of the latest-flowering of Robert Gartrell's Robin Hill azaleas and useful for extending bloom season after earlier evergreen azaleas have finished. Its compact, spreading habit matches the rest of the Robin Hill group, bred for cold hardiness and large flowers on a smaller plant than Southern Indica types. Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and prune right after flowering to preserve next year's buds.
sources: Journal of the American Rhododendron Society

common_name: Lady Louise Azalea (Pink Blotched Robin Hill Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Lady Louise is a Robin Hill azalea bred from 'Louise Gable' x 'Tama-giku' with pink, darker-blotched single flowers.

directions: Lady Louise was bred by Robert Gartrell from a cross of 'Louise Gable' and 'Tama-giku', producing 3-inch pink single flowers with a darker blotch in late May on a compact, low-growing Robin Hill plant. It shares the group's broad, overlapping petals and glossy dark foliage, giving a full, rounded flower face unusual among compact hardy azaleas. Site in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and prune immediately after bloom since flower buds form on the current season's growth.
sources: Journal of the American Rhododendron Society

common_name: Dorothy Hayden Azalea (White Flat-Faced Robin Hill Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Dorothy Hayden is a Robin Hill azalea with large, flat-faced white flowers and a pale green throat.

directions: Dorothy Hayden bears large, 3.5-inch, flat-faced white single flowers with a pale green throat in early June, among the latest of the Robin Hill azaleas to bloom. Its broad, overlapping petals give an especially full-faced flower typical of Gartrell's breeding goals, set against the compact, glossy-leaved habit shared across the Robin Hill line. Grow in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and prune right after flowering since buds for next spring set soon afterward.
sources: Journal of the American Rhododendron Society

common_name: Early Beni Azalea (Pale Scarlet Early-Blooming Robin Hill Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Early Beni is the earliest-blooming of the common Robin Hill azaleas, opening pale scarlet hose-in-hose blooms in early May.

directions: Early Beni opens pale scarlet, 2.5-inch hose-in-hose double flowers in early May, well ahead of most other Robin Hill azaleas, giving an early show of color on a compact, low-mounding plant. It carries the same cold-hardy breeding and glossy dark foliage typical of Robert Gartrell's Robin Hill line, bred to combine large flowers with a smaller, denser habit than Southern Indica azaleas. Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and prune immediately after bloom to protect next year's flower buds.
sources: Journal of the American Rhododendron Society

common_name: Red Slippers Azalea (Reblooming Red Back Acres Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Red Slippers is a Back Acres hybrid that reliably reblooms in fall in addition to its main spring flush.

directions: Red Slippers is one of B.Y. Morrison's Back Acres hybrids, bred at his Pass Christian, Mississippi garden, and is notable among older azalea cultivars for its lightly scented, bright reddish-pink to red, trumpet-shaped single to semi-double flowers that bloom heavily in spring and rebloom again in fall. Its glossy foliage and 3-4 foot rounded habit make it a dependable, long-blooming choice for Gulf Coast borders and foundation plantings. Grow in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and water deeply during dry spells to support the fall rebloom.
sources: Journal of the American Rhododendron Society (Cold Hardiness of Robin Hill, Holly Springs and Back Acres Hybrid Azalea Selections)

common_name: White Jade Azalea (Ruffled Pale Green-Flushed White Back Acres Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; White Jade is a Back Acres hybrid with ruffled white flowers flushed pale green on the upper lobes, from a cross of 'Helen Gunning' x 'Rei Ro'.

directions: White Jade is one of B.Y. Morrison's Back Acres hybrids, raised at his Pass Christian, Mississippi garden, bearing 3-inch ruffled flowers that open white and carry a soft pale green flush on the upper lobes through its May bloom period. The ruffled petal edges give the flowers extra texture compared to flatter-faced white azaleas, and the plant keeps a rounded, medium-sized evergreen habit well suited to Gulf Coast shade gardens. Grow in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and prune right after flowering since buds for the following year set soon afterward.
sources: Journal of the American Rhododendron Society

common_name: Ivan Anderson Azalea (White-Centered Rose-Pink Double Back Acres Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Ivan Anderson is a Back Acres hybrid bred by B.Y. Morrison from a cross of 'Warai Gishi' x 'Horaku' crossed again with 'Kokoku'.

directions: Ivan Anderson is a Back Acres hybrid bred by B.Y. Morrison at his Pass Christian, Mississippi garden. Its nearly 3-inch double flowers show white centers bordered by a broad band of vivid to deep purplish-red, giving a bold two-tone effect distinct from the single-color flowers of most older evergreen azaleas. The plant keeps a rounded, medium evergreen habit well adapted to the Deep South heat and humidity where Morrison bred it. Grow in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and prune immediately after bloom to preserve next year's buds.
sources: Journal of the American Rhododendron Society

common_name: Margaret Douglas Azalea (Coral-Edged Pink Back Acres Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Margaret Douglas is a Back Acres hybrid that spreads wider than tall if given room, with a bold coral picotee edge.

directions: Margaret Douglas is a Back Acres hybrid bred by B.Y. Morrison, bearing 3-inch single flowers that are soft pink on the inside with a distinctive broad picotee band of coral along the outer edge. Reaching about 4 feet tall in ten years, it tends to spread wider than it grows tall when given room, making it useful as a broad, informal specimen or loose mass planting. Grow in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and prune right after flowering since flower buds for the following spring set on the current season's growth.
sources: University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Plant of the Week

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil at a woodland edge with morning sun and afternoon shade; Harrison's Red is an unusually coral-colored selection of the normally yellow-flowered Florida azalea, discovered near Chipley, Florida.

directions: Harrison's Red was discovered growing wild near Chipley, Florida and selected for its unusual coral-red flower color, a striking departure from the clear yellow to orange-gold tones typical of the Florida azalea species. Like the straight species, it opens its fragrant, long-stamened trumpets in early to mid-spring before or as the leaves emerge, drawing early pollinators to the woodland edge. It keeps the same tall, airy, multi-stemmed habit and excellent Gulf South heat tolerance of wild R. austrinum populations. Site in humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil with morning sun and afternoon shade, and avoid heavy pruning since flower buds form on the previous season's wood.
sources: Jenkins Arboretum Native Azalea Conservation Collection

common_name: Chipola River Florida Azalea (Clear Yellow Wild Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil at a woodland edge with morning sun and afternoon shade; Chipola River is a clear-yellow wild selection of the Florida azalea found along its namesake river.

directions: Chipola River was discovered growing wild along the Chipola River in the Florida panhandle and selected for its clear, consistent yellow flower color, a more uniform tone than the yellow-to-orange range typical of wild Florida azalea populations. It opens its fragrant, flared, long-stamened trumpets in early to mid-spring, typically just before or as the new leaves emerge. The shrub retains the tall, open, multi-stemmed form and strong Gulf Coast heat tolerance of the species it was selected from. Grow in humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil at a woodland edge with morning sun and afternoon shade, pruning minimally and only right after bloom.
sources: Jenkins Arboretum Native Azalea Conservation Collection

common_name: Mary Brooke Alabama Azalea (Pale Yellow Fragrant Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Mary Brooke is a pale yellow selection of the normally white-flowered Alabama azalea, held in the Native Rhododendron Germplasm Repository at Jenkins Arboretum.

directions: Mary Brooke is a soft, pale yellow-flowered selection of the Alabama azalea, a species whose wild populations almost always bloom white with a yellow blotch, making this a distinctive color break within the species. Its fragrant spring flowers open on bare or barely leafing stems, carrying the same clove-like scent prized in the straight species. The suckering, colony-forming habit and Gulf Coast heat tolerance match wild R. alabamense, making it a good choice for naturalizing at a woodland edge. Site in humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade and avoid heavy pruning, since flower buds form on the previous year's growth.
sources: Jenkins Arboretum Native Azalea Conservation Collection

common_name: Varnadoe's Phlox Pink Piedmont Azalea (Dark Pink Fragrant Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Varnadoe's Phlox Pink holds a richer, more consistent dark pink than typical wild Piedmont azalea populations.

directions: Selected by a Georgia grower named Varnadoe, this is one of the darkest and most reliably colored pink selections of the Piedmont azalea, a species whose wild flowers vary widely from nearly white to pale pink. In early spring it opens showy, fragrant, tubular flowers in a rich, consistent dark pink, with the long curving stamens and sweet honeysuckle-like scent typical of the species, appearing before or as new leaves emerge. It keeps the vigorous, upright, multi-stemmed habit of wild R. canescens and tolerates Gulf South heat and humidity well, blooming heavily even on young plants. Grow in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade.
sources: Jenkins Arboretum Native Azalea Conservation Collection
